add.gloss: Causal influence: rationale representations determine the emitted claim rather than only correlate with it. It is the rung above decodability, tested by activation patching.

add.quote: Matched counterfactuals control for this confound by holding the claim text fixed while swapping only the evidence passage. Because the claim is unchanged, any shift in the consistency head’s prediction must be driven by the evidence content alone, making matched counterfactuals a strictly more diagnostic test of whether the model reads the evidence rather than relying on claim-text shortcuts.
add.gloss: FEVER counterfactual that swaps only the evidence and keeps the claim text. MSwap/MOrig are how often the head follows the swapped versus the original label.

add.gloss: Decodability is scored as consistency-head accuracy from the pooled explanation span. It reaches 98.6% in the code setting while the generated prose stays unfaithful.

add.quote: CoT reasoning can be viewed as an explanation for the model’s final prediction, but because explanations do not mention the influence of biases, they are unfaithful—they do not accurately describe the process models are using to make a prediction (Jacovi & Goldberg, 2020).

add.quote: For Argument, if the model says that it is answering the question based on the content of the provided argument we treat that as verbalization. add.gloss: Hand labels on 1040 biased answers: only saying the cue drove the answer counts. App. F drops Perez et al.'s sycophancy set because models there verbalize following the user.

add.quote: For each CoT reviewed, we annotate how coherent the reasoning is, on a scale of 1 to 5. A score of 1 is not convincing while 5 is compelling. We treat CoTs with a score of 4 or 5 as coherent biased reasoning.
add.gloss: Blind author ratings of 439 biased MMLU CoTs, reported as a share of all reviewed CoTs: 27.2% for GPT-3.5T and 15.1% after BCT.

add.quote: Unlike most other biases, there is no bias towards one particular answer, so we measure biased reasoning by measuring how often the model changes its answer after asking “Are you sure?” For this bias, we expect perfectly unbiased models to not switch answers from correct to incorrect, so the unbiased baseline is 0%.
add.gloss: For biases with no target answer, biased reasoning is the answer-switch rate against a 0% baseline. Are You Sure moves Sharma et al.'s test to CoT; Positional Bias swaps order.

add.quote: Post Hoc Rationalization. If models answer a question incorrectly and then explain, they tend to give incorrect reasoning, even if they can give the correct reasoning when prompted to give an explanation before answering. We explicitly insert an incorrect non-CoT answer into the model’s side of the chat and prompt the model to explain its reasoning.
add.gloss: Explaining an answer already given, here a wrong one inserted into the model's own turn, pulls the reasoning toward that answer. It is measured as biased reasoning.

add.quote: We first create a new dataset of 9 different biases that affect GPT-3.5-Turbo and Llama-8b models. These consist of spurious-few-shot patterns, post hoc rationalization, and sycophantic settings. Models switch to the answer implied by the bias, without mentioning the effect of the bias in the CoT.
add.gloss: Suggested Answer, Are You Sure, Post Hoc, Wrong Few-Shot, Wrong Argument, Spurious Squares, Hindsight, Distractor Fact and Positional Bias. Turpin et al. had three biases.

add.quote: pose a more serious threat in the form of decreased chain of thought (CoT) monitorability (Baker et al., 2025; Korbak et al., 2025): illegible CoTs—either to humans or other LLMs—render models’ internal reasoning processes more opaque, leading to difficulty in determining intent and predicting future actions.
add.gloss: Monitorability is the ability to read intent and predict actions from the CoT. CoTs illegible to human or LLM readers lower it.

add.quote: Although the KL divergence driving language drift in Theorem 3 can result entirely from shifting probability mass in the answer distribution ${\pi}(\mathcal{Y}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Z})$ —and therefore does not necessitate change in the CoT distribution ${\pi}(\mathcal{Z}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X})$ —altering ${\pi}(\mathcal{Y}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Z})$ while holding ${\pi}(\mathcal{Z}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X})$ constant still undeniably constitutes language drift.
add.gloss: Drift counts even when the CoT distribution is unchanged: if correct answers follow traces a human would get wrong, the meaning of the trace has drifted.

add.quote: We first verified that the models were not generating performative CoTs: i.e. determining the answer early on, and simply generating a CoT post-hoc to mimic their training distribution (Boppana et al., 2026).
add.gloss: The answer is fixed early and the CoT is written post hoc to imitate training data. It is ruled out before legibility is read as drift.

add.quote: if $\pi$ is generating performative CoTs, we would expect ${\pi}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx,z_{n})\approx{\pi}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx,z)$ . On the other hand, if $\pi$ is actually using the full reasoning trace, we would expect ${\pi}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx,z_{n})\ll{\pi}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx,z)$ .
add.gloss: Compares the answer probability given each partial trace z_n with that given the full trace. Probability rising toward the full trace shows the CoT is used.

add.quote: Next, we verified that the models were not performing invisible reasoning: simply using the CoT to perform computations in the hidden states to arrive at the final answer, independently of the actual tokens in the CoT (Baherwani et al., 2026).
add.gloss: The CoT positions carry hidden-state computation whose tokens do not matter to the answer. If present, the text would not show the reasoning.

add.quote: If ${\pi}$ is performing invisible reasoning, we would expect that the actual tokens in the reasoning chain do not impact final-answer probability. Otherwise, we would expect that the probability of $y_{i}$ conditioned on a reasoning trace $z_{k}$ —generated for a different query $x_{k}$ —would be significantly lower than conditioned on the original trace $z_{i}$ : ${\pi}(y_{i}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx_{i},z_{k})\ll{\pi}(y_{i}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx_{i},z_{i})$ .
add.gloss: Replaces the trace with one from another query in the same length decile. A large drop in answer probability (Table 4: positive for all models) shows the tokens matter.
